stories.headline: Hockey World Cup: England exposes India’s shortcomings
stories.deck: The European side rallies to score a 4-2 win and advances to the second round; Harmanpreet & Co. lack ideas and composure inside the circle
stories.bodyText:
The visuals, under the gloomy skies here at the Wagener Stadion, painted quite the picture.
Late in the third quarter, England came from behind to regain the lead when Henry Croft, under little pressure from Jugraj Singh, had the time and space to receive the ball, take a few touches, turn and fire it past Mohith H.S. Before the restart, the rolling subs were called for and Jugraj, once again, showed no urgency to get off the pitch, forcing head coach Craig Fulton to furiously give him the marching orders.
After the opening day win, where there were still several questions left to be answered, the Indian men’s team failed to come up with them in its World Cup Pool-D 4-2 defeat at the hands of No. 3-ranked England on Monday.
Coming into the tournament, England boasted the best defensive record of the year.
In its 17 matches, it conceded just a goal per game, a remarkable number by hockey standards.
Yet, India recovered from the Nicholas Bandurak opener to score two, one from a Harmanpreet Singh rocket drag-flick and another from forward Dilpreet Singh, after some neat work from Hardik Singh and Abhishek Nain by the byline.
Tough going
But as it did in the first quarter, India struggled against England’s man-to-man full court press, which forced turnovers in compromising areas of the pitch. England’s pressure paid off in the 38th minute when Stuart Rushmere stretched to get on the end of Liam Sanford’s fired in pass as the ball sailed past Mohith. A few minutes later, Mohith looked on helplessly as Croft added a third to make it 3-2.
India showed urgency in the fourth quarter, but even as England had two green card penalties, it lacked ideas and composure inside the circle to find a reply.
Killer blow
Bandurak, who had earlier capitalised on a defensive lapse for his first goal, piled on India’s misery when he fired home from a penalty corner to take England to the second round. While India could still reach the next round, this result will only make its path to the semifinals harder.
The Indian women’s team will face off against South Africa on Tuesday.
The result: India 2 (Harmanpreet 16-pc, Dilpreet 24) lost to England 4 (Bandurak 13 & 54-pc, Rushmere 38, Croft 42).

stories.headline: From career-threatening injury to Masters triumph, Chaliha’s Korean journey comes full circle
stories.deck: Ashmita Chaliha’s comeback from a serious knee injury has taken her from a career low outside the world’s top 200 to winning the Korea Masters title this year. After months of mentally difficult rehabilitation, she returned through smaller tournaments to regain fitness and confidence. Her title triumph reflects patience and resilience, as she rebuilt her career one match at a time.
stories.bodyText:
New Delhi: There was a time when Ashmita Chaliha could only watch while fellow players were training, travelling and discussing their next tournaments.
The Assam shuttler was confined to rehabilitation for a career-threatening medial meniscus tear in her right knee that she sustained during the 2024 
Korea Open
 in Aug. She was repeating the same exercises day after day. Her racquet was largely out of reach, her competitive rhythm gone and her ranking slipped rapidly.
For someone who had been ranked inside the world’s top 40, the slide was particularly painful. Ashmita eventually found herself outside the top 200, a point she describes as her “rock bottom”.
But that low eventually became the starting point of a comeback that reached its latest high at Korea Masters this year, where she had a memorable run to claim the title on Aug 9.
Looking back at the difficult period, Ashmita admitted that the biggest battle was not necessarily physical. “Preparing during my injury, like for rehab and stuff, it was more mentally than physically,” she said.
“I was always doing the same thing while there was training and stuff. It was upsetting because you see other players preparing for the tournament and discussing the next plan, whereas I was just stuck there,” Ashmita recalled.
Yet somewhere amid frustration and uncertainty, she found a different kind of motivation. 
She had little control over how quickly her body would recover, but she could control how she approached the road back.
The first objective was not immediately to win a major title or chase a ranking. It was simply to find out whether she could compete again.
Once she was cleared to return, she chose to ease herself back through smaller tournaments. The matches were as much a test of her physical condition as they were of her confidence.
“Once I started to play, I was mostly getting back with small tournaments. I just wanted to know how fit I am or if I can compete with the good players,” she said.
Those early tournaments helped rebuild something an injury can take away from an athlete just as quickly as fitness and belief.
The Korea Open triumph was therefore more than another title on her resume. It represented the distance she had travelled from those lonely rehabilitation sessions, from watching others compete while she waited for her own opportunity.
On making the comeback after losing the first game in the Korea Masters final, Ashmita said, “I was just in the game and taking one point at a time. I wasn’t thinking about whether I could win the match. I was just playing and seeing what happens. When I changed sides, it was better for me and my attack was going pretty well, so I stuck to that game.”
There was no overnight transformation. Her return was built through patience, smaller competitions and the willingness to start again.
And that is perhaps what makes the Korea Masters victory particularly significant. Ashmita did not simply return to the winner’s circle; she returned after experiencing how quickly an athlete can fall when injury takes away the one thing they live for and that is competition.
She may not be part of India’s World Championships campaign in New Delhi this time, but her Korea Open triumph has offered a timely reminder of what she is capable of when healthy and confident.
Playing at home can be a double-edged sword, the 26-year-old admitted. “It’s a mixed feeling. Firstly, it’s in your home country, so you want to win and get a medal for India,” she said. “That already builds a little bit of pressure, but it’s also very exciting to play in front of your home crowd. There will be additional support, and you wouldn’t want to let people down.”
For an athlete who once felt stuck on the sidelines, the journey back has been about learning to move forward one tournament at a time. The rankings may have fallen, the road may have been frustratingly long, but Ashmita has shown that a career can be rebuilt from its lowest point. Sometimes, the comeback begins when all you can do is believe that your time will come.

briefs.headline: Facing the No. 1 challenge
briefs.bodyText:
Two players barely into their twenties faced the same daunting task at the World championships: take down a World No. 1. By the end of the day, one had turned it into a three-game thriller while the other discovered how ruthless the world’s best can be.
The 21-year-old Ayush Shetty relishes the pressure and the big stage. Against China’s Shi Yuqi, he raced to 17-6 in the final game and left the Chinese clueless.
Ayush was on the cusp of registering the biggest win of his fledgling career. The defending champion then clawed back. The comfortable lead became a slender one, and the fans experienced nervous moments as Ayush tried to finish what he had started.
Prophetic
Coach Sagar Chopda had seen it coming. “He is playing in India and on our home court... the pressure is going to be on Shi Yuqi,” Sagar had said before the tournament. It proved prophetic.
The 20-year-old Kaloyana Nalbantova battled it out with the other World No. 1, An Se-young. The Bulgarian had called her opponent “the best” and described the draw as “the hardest first round one can get”.
While Ayush’s match threatened to unravel, Se-young’s barely became a contest. She won in straight games, leaving Nalbantova to admire how far the world’s best were.
The Bulgarian, however, accepted it with no bitterness. “I had the best experience one can have,” she said.

briefs.deck: The left-handers put on 146 for the sixth wicket as Sri Lanka ends up with 284 in its first innings in response to the visitor’s 462; Suthar claims a four-for while fellow left-arm spinner Jadeja scalps three
briefs.bodyText:
Under largely clear skies, Sonal Dinusha shone bright. The Sri Lankan batter’s century helped the host stretch its first innings even as India’s 462 remained beyond reach. Sri Lanka scored 284, conceded a 178-run lead before dark clouds rolled in and concluded the third day of the first Test at the Galle International Stadium.
On Monday, Sri Lanka’s first innings was a tale of two parts. The initial blend of quick runs and fast dismissals evident from 90 for five was followed by a period of stability as Dinusha (100, 168b, 4x4, 2x6) and Niroshan Dickwella (80, 115b, 7x4) shared a 146-run sixth-wicket partnership. The duo batted through the second session to offer some cheer to the local fans thronging the grass-banks and the ramparts of the Dutch fort.
Dickwella swept against spin, Dinusha remained industrious and the two southpaws frustrated Shubman Gill’s men. Manav Suthar, who was the pick among the bowlers, was attacked as Dinusha hoisted a six and Dickwella, as was largely the norm through his tenure, swept past the ropes. Between lunch and tea, the two added 116 runs.
In the day’s last session, India began to find its way back as Prasidh Krishna grazed Dickwella’s bat and helped Rishabh Pant exult behind the stumps. Keshara Nuwantha’s drive was deflected off Yashasvi Jaiswal at silly point, and the rebound was easily pouched by Gill at cover. But Dinusha moved on with a reverse-swept four off Kuldeep Yadav and soon his maiden Test century was etched. The tail wilted around him and he, too, fell to Ravindra Jadeja.
Earlier, under bright skies, resuming at the overnight 460 for nine, India added a mere two more and lasted just four deliveries as Prasidh edged Asitha Fernando. The Sri Lankan batting response seemed fixated on hustling the runs at a fluent rate even if wickets tumbled.
Opener Nishan Fernando nibbled at a short delivery from Mohammed Siraj and found Devdutt Padikkal waiting in the slips. Sri Lanka was yet to open its account and Lahiru Udara with Dinesh Chandimal, tried to seal the crack. Udara played his shots, punching a four off Siraj.
However, when Suthar was pressed into service, Chandimal feathered his first delivery to an alert Pant. Suthar, a classical left-arm spinner, found turn and bounce. Meanwhile, the hosts motored on with Kamindu Mendis pulling a six off Prasidh. The medley of runs and dismissals seemed to be on a repetitive loop as Udara slashed Suthar straight to backward-point.
Gill used Suthar and Kuldeep in tandem for a while. The latter was driven well by host skipper Dhananjaya de Silva. Kuldeep got a wicket too, thanks largely to a piece of fielding brilliance by Gill. Mendis chipped up a drive, and as the ball dipped, Gill dived and plucked an outstanding left-handed catch. Perhaps the ambidextrous catching drills ahead of this match, helped.
Dhananjaya edged Jadeja, and the next man, Dickwella, struck two fours, and at lunch, Sri Lanka mustered 99 for five. As the day progressed the host found a toehold even as it unravelled in the final stretch.

briefs.headline: Jagadeesan and Shahrukh open up about challenges
briefs.bodyText:
As seasoned Tamil Nadu cricketers, N. Jagadeesan and Shahrukh Khan have weathered the full spectrum of the sport’s highs and lows.
Ahead of their Tuesday’s TNPL match, the Chepauk Super Gillies skipper and his Vida Kovai Kings counterpart gave elaborate and veracious answers to the challenges in their roles and careers.
Commenting on his role as a finisher, Shahrukh said: “I am 31 now. And as a batter, when I was in my mid-20s, it [reflecting on his innings] felt completely different. But that’s the sport. No matter how set you are, it’s just a one-ball game… some days it comes off, and some days it doesn’t.”
Shahrukh touched upon the accolades and criticisms that come with being a middle-order batter.
“The toughest job is to play down the order. On days you do well, you are applauded more than anybody else. But on days when you don’t do well, you are put down more than anyone.”
Handling failures
On how he handles failures, Shahrukh added: “As a finisher, I need to have a good relationship with myself. Because no matter what, the most important thing is how you feel about yourself.”
Jagadeesan gave his perspective on life as a cricketer, and more specifically the nuances in shifting approaches in different formats.
“To put that in simple terms, I am okay to accept failure. The moment I’m not able to accept failure, it becomes very difficult to express myself. In this format, there could be a lot of failures, and that’s one thing that I’ve [told myself],” he said.
“The relationship with failure comes from the love for the game. I started playing because I love the sport… and as you go on this professional journey, you stop enjoying the sport as it is, thinking about your selections and whatnot. In the end, it is just about you having faith in yourself”.

briefs.headline: Badminton World Championships | Giant-killer Ayush sends Shi packing
briefs.bodyText:
Ayush Shetty, ahead of his badminton World championships debut against defending champion and World No. 1 Shi Yuqi, had assured: “Tomorrow is a new day, and it will be a different game.”
The youngster made good on his promise, sending the Chinese star packing on Monday for the biggest upset of the day and perhaps the entire tournament. He won 21-14, 13-21, 21-19 in 73 minutes despite a late surge from Shi that almost derailed his dream start.
With Ayush leading 17-6 in the decider, the match looked all wrapped up. But Shi stepped up, produced a few impeccable smashes that landed on the line and came up with delectable drops to make it 19-20.
For all the drama, the end was marked by the softest of returns to the back of the court, leaving Shi stranded at the net. The Indian, drained to even celebrate, sported only a slight smile.
Having lost the three previous meetings, including the Asia Championships final in April, Ayush was clearly prepared for Shi.
He started aggressively and did not allow his more fancied opponent to control the momentum.
The 21-year-old took an early lead, a sequence that included the longest rally of the match (45 shots) at 8-5. Shi kept hitting wide and over even as Ayush dived all over the court, fighting for every point. Taking full advantage of his height, the Indian mixed his jump smashes with soft net play.
But to Shi’s credit, he gradually grew into the match, but Ayush was never overwhelmed.
With Shi and his coach indulging in animated discussions during every break, the Chinese was not in full control of either his game or emotions. Despite an attempted comeback, he eventually bowed out.
Ayush’s win was the highlight of the Indian challenge on a day when the rest of the home hopefuls, including P.V. Sindhu, breezed through to the next round. Sindhu went past Ireland’s Sophia Noble 21-7, 21-11.
In doubles, Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand took just over half an hour for a 21-9, 21-13 win over Paula Lopez and Lucia Rodriguez of Spain while Kavipriya Selvam and Simran Singhi beat another Spanish pair, Nikol Carulla and Carmen Maria Jimenez, 22-20, 21-14.
Hariharan Amsakarunan and M.R. Arjun were leading 21-16, 6-4 when their Irish opponents Scott Guildea and Paul Reynolds conceded.

briefs.headline: Durand Cup: Bagan edges Jamshedpur on penalties, books semifinal spot
briefs.bodyText:
Mohun Bagan Super Giant edged past Jamshedpur FC 9-8 on penalties after being locked 1-1 in regulation time to reach the semifinals of the 135th Durand Cup at Salt Lake Stadium here on Monday.
Sahal Abdul Samad put Bagan ahead in the second minute, but Devendra Murgaonkar equalised towards the end of the first half. With the tournament regulations having no provision for extra-time, the quarterfinal went straight to a penalty shootout.
Both teams converted their first five attempts, forcing sudden-death. The first 16 kicks were successful before Jamshedpur’s young Lawmsangzuala saw his effort saved by Bagan goalkeeper Vishal Kaith when the teams were tied 8-8. Tekcham Abhishek Singh, then, converted the decisive penalty.
Bagan struggled in the attacking third and managed to keep only eight shots on target despite making 24 attempts at the opponent goal. Jamshedpur, which announced the dissolution of the club during the tournament, put up a spirited fight with an all-Indian team but sadly had to bow out.
Defending champion NorthEast United FC advanced to the semifinals with a 5-2 comeback win over Shillong Lajong FC in the fourth quarterfinal at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, Shillong.
Moroccan striker Alaaeddine Ajaraie scored a hat-trick, his second of the tournament, while Spaniard Etyan Gonzalez and Jithin M.S. added one each.
Shillong Lajong led 2-1 at half-time. However, NorthEast United came back strongly and set up a semifinal clash with Bagan at the same venue on Thursday.

briefs.headline: ‘Show composure’: Fulton’s message to India ahead of must-not-lose Pakistan clash
briefs.deck: Following India's defeat in the Hockey World Cup, coach Craig Fulton emphasised the necessity for stricter defensive discipline. He urged players to maintain composure and enhance their defensive strategies ahead of the critical match against Pakistan. Midfielder Manpreet Singh echoed his sentiments, pinpointing defensive errors as pivotal to their loss. A point against Pakistan is essential for…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India head coach Craig Fulton has urged his side to show greater composure and sharpen their defensive discipline against Pakistan after 
England exposed their weaknesses in a 2-4 defeat in their second Pool D match
 of the Hockey World Cup on Monday.
India produced a strong first half and led 2-1 at the break after goals from 
Harmanpreet Singh
 and Dilpreet Singh. But England turned the contest around after half-time, scoring three times to leave India needing at least a point against Pakistan in their final pool match on Wednesday to progress to the second round.
Fulton admitted India’s defensive intensity dropped after the interval.
“The first half was good. We got PCs on the counter-attack and came back nicely with a bit more control. In the third quarter our defence was not as good as it was supposed to be,” Fulton said after the match.
“England played like a world number three team. We created a few chances but couldn't convert those.”
Fulton calls for composure against Pakistan
The India coach was quick to shift focus to the Pakistan game, recognising the importance of Wednesday’s clash. India have three points from two matches after beating Wales in their opener, while Pakistan have one point.
“If we had won today, we still have to do the business in the next game. We just have to be better on the ball in the final match and show a bit of composure. We needed to press out and put some pressure on them,” he said.
“The forward line played well but we needed to score three-plus goals and we could only score two. It's just the second match and we will learn from this loss. We have another big opportunity against Pakistan and the boys are motivated for that.”
India had taken control of the contest after falling behind in the first quarter. Nicholas Bandurak put England ahead in the 14th minute before Harmanpreet equalised from a penalty corner. Dilpreet then completed the turnaround in the second quarter.
England, however, dominated the third quarter. Stuart Rushmere levelled in the 39th minute before Henry Croft put England ahead four minutes later. Bandurak added his second from a penalty corner in the 55th minute to seal the victory.
Manpreet stresses defensive discipline
Experienced midfielder 
Manpreet Singh
 also pointed to defensive lapses as a key reason for the defeat and warned India cannot afford similar mistakes against Pakistan.
“We were playing so well till the third quarter but there were a few defensive lapses in the last quarter which cost us. Overall, the performance was good but the defence has to be very strong against the top teams and we need to convert our chances also,” Manpreet said.
India tried several variations from penalty corners, but England’s defence stood firm.
“We were trying variations on PCs but they defended well. We cannot underestimate any team. Pakistan also have good penalty corner specialists, so we must not concede PCs against them. We have to earn more PCs in the upcoming matches,” he said.
Manpreet also stressed that India continued to create opportunities despite England’s pressure.
“Our defenders broke their full press many times. It's a long tournament and we will learn from the mistakes. You cannot play with the same momentum for the whole 60 minutes, but we are creating opportunities till the last minute. There is a structure of playing and we follow that,” he said.
With England now sitting at the top of Pool D with two wins, India’s attention turns firmly to Pakistan. A draw would be enough to take India through, while defeat would end their campaign.

briefs.headline: Hockey WC: Marijne questions FIH over China’s penalty stroke, later deletes posts
briefs.deck: Indian women's hockey coach questioned the penalty-stroke rule interpretation after a draw. He shared footage and sought clarification from the International Hockey Federation. Former players also expressed their views on the controversial penalty-stroke action. The coach later removed his social media posts regarding the incident. FIH had not responded to clarification requests at the time of…
briefs.bodyText:
A day after the Indian women’s hockey team held China to a 2-2 draw in their World Cup opener at Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen, Netherlands, coach Sjoerd Marijne questioned the interpretation of the penalty-stroke rule by the International Hockey Federation’s (FIH) Rules Committee.
Marijne took to social media to share footage of China’s Ying Zhang taking the penalty stroke from three different angles, questioning whether the action constituted a “dragging” action, which is not permitted under the rules.
“Good to know, this is apparently NOT dragging. The reaction of the rules committee from the FIH after asking clarification is that this clip of the penalty stroke is not dragging. I have just asked it for clarification what to tell my players,” Marijne wrote.
Zhang’s penalty stroke came in the dying seconds of the first half and helped China draw level after India had taken the lead through Navneet Kaur. China eventually held on for a 2-2 draw.
According to Article 13.7(i) of the FIH Rules of Hockey, “The player taking the penalty stroke must push, flick or scoop the ball and is permitted to raise it to any height. Using a ‘dragging’ action to play the ball at a penalty stroke is not permitted.”
The distinction between a flick and a drag, however, appeared to be at the heart of Marijne’s concern. By sharing the footage and seeking clarification from the rules committee, the Dutchman had raised questions over how the rule is interpreted and communicated to teams and players.
Former Netherlands international goalkeeper Jaap Stockmann, who was present at the stadium, felt the action did appear to resemble a drag. “Indeed, it looked like a short drag. I was in the stadium and that’s the first thing I thought,” Stockmann told TOI.
Chris Ciriello, former Australian international and one of the world’s leading drag-flickers, also felt the action “looked like a drag”.
“Technically, the ball has to move in one direction and it must be one movement. We had a goal disallowed in the semifinal against Germany at London Olympics because one of our players dragged the ball,” Ciriello told TOI.
“It is unfortunate, but my rule to my players is that there is enough time and opportunity across the whole match not to focus only on one decision. Be disciplined, take control of your chances and don’t leave it to the umpires.”
He did, however, add: “They (India) played well. Exciting to see what they can achieve.”
Marijne later deleted the posts from both Instagram and X.
FIH, however, responded to TOI’s request for clarification on what constitutes a dragging action during. “A dragging action occurs when the player moves the ball along the ground with the stick for a discernible distance before releasing it. This is characteristic of the drag component of a drag-flick and is not permitted when taking a penalty stroke,” FIH said in a reply to TOI.
“The distinction is not determined solely by the length or shape of the stick movement. Umpires consider whether the ball is propelled from its stationary position as part of the push or flick, or whether it is first moved along the ground with the stick through a discernible part of the action before being released. The movement of the ball in relation to the player’s stance and body may also assist in making that judgement.”
FIH clarification suggests that the key consideration is not simply the apparent movement of the stick, but whether the ball itself is moved along the ground for a discernible distance before being released.
